title: 20 days of compute vs 7 hours: rethinking what state-of-the-art means — Bertrand Charpentier, Pruna

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central object is evaluation methodology—comparing leaderboards, analyzing win rates, critiquing metrics like CLIP score, and proposing Pareto fronts as a benchmarking tool for image generation models. The benchmarking methodology is general-purpose while the evaluated models are image generation and editing systems in the media and creative domain. The talk focuses on the evaluation phase and discusses compression-based optimization as a secondary theme. Requires familiarity with Elo scores, win rates, and model compression concepts but remains accessible to a broad engineering audience. summary: Charpentier frames the question of which AI model is truly 'state of the art' and notes it is more confusing than people assume. Two common methods—checking public leaderboards and performing internal evaluation—both naively lead to selecting a large foundation model. On leaderboards, LM Arena, Design Arena, and Artificial Analysis produce different rankings for image editing; the same model can move from rank 10 to rank 5 across boards, and Elo score ranges differ. Aggregated leaderboard scores hide per-task performance: ChatGPT image, while top overall, is never top-one in specific sub-tasks like object removal or background changes. Leaderboards are built on only a few thousand samples, and no model achieves near-100% win rates—most lose at least 40% of head-to-head battles, meaning the top-ranked model is wrong for roughly 40% of real use cases. For internal evaluation, manual inspection introduces dual bias: personal preference and small sample size. Automated metrics like CLIP score produce inconsistent rankings across datasets with tiny score variations. Task-specific metrics (e.g., text-rendering metrics) yield more consistent and discriminating rankings. Charpentier then demonstrates that quality is compute-driven: Design Arena's 26K-battle evaluation of ChatGPT image took 20 days of compute, cost $5,000, and consumed ~556 kWh—energy equivalent to 400 marathons. A compressed Pruna model completed the same evaluation in 7 hours for $265, requiring only ~4 marathons of energy. His central proposal is the Pareto front: plotting quality (e.g., Elo score) against an efficiency metric (latency or price) reveals not one but three or four state-of-the-art models clustered tightly in quality but varying up to 20x in efficiency. Task-specific Pareto fronts (e.g., text rendering) surface optimized small models that remain on the frontier for specific use cases. Benchmarking is not dead, he argues, but done properly it surfaces small specialized models rather than large foundation models. During Q&A he describes compression methods including per-module quantization, pruning, and reducing denoising steps via distillation or caching (from 50 down to 4-20 steps).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: What is state of the art?
sections.summary: Charpentier introduces the question of which AI model is state of the art, noting it is important but confusing, with people using two main methods: checking public leaderboards and performing internal evaluation. Both naively lead to picking large foundation models.

sections.title: Problem with public leaderboards: inconsistent rankings
sections.summary: Different leaderboards (LM Arena, Design Arena, Artificial Analysis) produce different rankings for image editing models. The same model shifts ranks across boards, Elo score ranges differ, and some models appear on only some leaderboards. The solution is to consult multiple leaderboards rather than trusting a single one.

sections.title: Problem with public leaderboards: aggregated scores vs. specific use cases
sections.summary: Leaderboard scores aggregate across many tasks, but per-use-case rankings differ significantly. ChatGPT image is never top-one in specific sub-task rankings—different models excel at different tasks. Users should target leaderboards matching their specific use case.

sections.title: Problem with public leaderboards: statistical significance and win rates
sections.summary: Leaderboards are built on only a few thousand samples, which is low compared to production-scale inference. Win rates show no model approaches 100%, with most losing at least 40% of battles—meaning the top model is wrong for ~40% of use cases. Averaging over more samples and matching final conditions is recommended.

sections.title: Internal evaluation: manual inspection bias
sections.summary: Manual inspection introduces two biases: personal preference and limited sample size. Two audience polls demonstrate divergent preferences and changing minds, illustrating why manual inspection alone is insufficient and should be scaled with many evaluators.

sections.title: Internal evaluation: automated metric problems and task-specific alternatives
sections.summary: Generic metrics like CLIP score produce inconsistent rankings across datasets with tiny score variations. Task-specific metrics (e.g., text-rendering metrics) yield more consistent rankings with larger discriminating differences. Understanding what a metric measures is essential.

sections.title: Quality is driven by compute: the cost of evaluation
sections.summary: Charpentier shows that quality evaluation is compute-intensive. Design Arena's 26K-battle evaluation took 20 days of compute, cost $5,000, and consumed ~556 kWh—energy equivalent to 400 marathons. A compressed Pruna model completed the same evaluation in 7 hours for $265, requiring only ~4 marathons of energy, generating images in under 1 second.

sections.title: Pareto fronts: multiple state-of-the-art models
sections.summary: Charpentier proposes the Pareto front as the tool for identifying state of the art. Plotting quality (Elo score) against efficiency (latency or price) reveals three or four state-of-the-art models clustered tightly in quality (1,100–1,200 Elo) but varying up to 20x in efficiency. Task-specific Pareto fronts (e.g., text rendering) surface optimized small models, demonstrated with flux models from BFL collaboration.

sections.title: Benchmarking done properly and Pruna's approach
sections.summary: Benchmarking is not dead but should be done properly: evaluate on many samples, match use-case conditions, and include efficiency. Proper evaluation surfaces small performant models rather than large foundation models. Pruna builds performance models served behind endpoints (1–5 seconds for image/video) and contributes open source compression tooling and research materials.

sections.title: Q&A: Compression methods
sections.summary: Charpentier describes compression families: per-module quantization, pruning of unimportant components, and reducing denoising steps from 20–50 down to 4–20 via distillation or caching. Pruna offers open source caching algorithms and internal algorithms for served models.
